article.title: Why More Data History Is Not Always Better for Prediction
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Using more historical data seems like an obvious way to improve a model. More rows can reduce variance and expose the model to more examples. But older data can also describe a business environment that no longer exists. Customer behavior, products, prices, channels, policies, and measurement systems change over time. A five-year training window may therefore mix several different regimes. The first question is whether the relationship between features and outcomes is stable. If customers used a payment method differently three years ago, those examples may teach patterns that are irrelevant today. Product launches and channel migrations can create similar breaks. Data definitions also change. A feature may have the same name but a different calculation after a system migration. Combining periods without checking lineage can introduce silent inconsistency. Recency weighting is one option. Recent observations receive more influence while older observations still contribute information. Another approach is to compare several rolling training windows and evaluate them on the same future period. This makes the trade-off between sample size and relevance visible. Rare events complicate the choice. When positive outcomes are scarce, a short window may contain too few examples for stable learning. In that case older data can be valuable, but teams should test whether the old positives resemble current ones. Segment composition matters as well. Growth in a new customer channel can make the latest population very different from the historical base. A model trained on long history may underrepresent that new segment. Seasonality should not be confused with obsolescence. A one-year window can miss unusual annual patterns, while several years can help estimate recurring seasonal effects. The appropriate horizon depends on the mechanism. Validation should always be time-aware. Randomly mixing old and new rows into train and test sets can hide temporal degradation. Training on earlier periods and testing on later periods better represents deployment. The goal is not to maximize the number of rows. It is to use enough relevant history to learn stable patterns without allowing obsolete regimes to dominate. Training-window length is therefore a model-design parameter that should be tested, documented, and monitored rather than chosen by habit.  Analysts should document the population, observation window, assumptions, and operational definition. This makes the conclusion reproducible and helps separate a headline result from the mechanism that produced it.
